findings.summary: A library catalog is a register of bibliographic items held by a library or library network, evolving from handwritten lists and clay tablets to card catalogs and modern online public access catalogs (OPACs). Its core objectives are to enable users to locate items by author, title, subject, or date; to show what the library holds by author, subject, or format; and to assist users in evaluating items by edition and character. While card catalogs were once ubiquitous, computerized cataloguing and OPACs have largely replaced them, though some informal usage of the term 'card catalog' persists for online systems. The largest international catalog is WorldCat, managed by OCLC, containing hundreds of millions of records representing billions of holdings.

mechanisms.title: Structured bibliographic indexing
mechanisms.explanation: The catalog organizes items using standardized fields such as author, title, subject, and publication date, allowing users to locate materials through explicit search criteria. This mechanism replaced earlier inflexible ledgers and enabled the expandability of card systems.

mechanisms.title: Physical and digital organization frameworks
mechanisms.explanation: Historically, catalog cards were stored in drawers and cabinets, later transitioning to computerized OPACs accessible via the web. This framework determines how items are physically or logically retrieved, shifting from card drawers to networked databases while preserving the goal of systematic access.

unknowns: The exact technical process by which early clay tablet or parchment lists were compiled and updated
